chapters.title: The Mystery of the Fortress
paragraphs: Durgar Hashya 283

Under the rule of the Company, the land had grown somewhat quiet. In Janakirama’s fortress, his fourth and fifth generation descendants still resided—Rajarama and his son Jayarama. Rajarama was an elderly man, his son Jayarama a youth. The household ran smoothly on the income from ancestral wealth and the surrounding zamindari. The accumulated fortune had not diminished over these generations; rather, it had increased. The descendants of Janakirama had a habit: as soon as money came into their hands, they would convert it into gold and keep it safe. In this way, piles of mohurs, asharfis, and ornaments had been hoarded. No one harbored any ill intent. In this wilderness, where was there room for luxury or vice?
Suddenly, the country was set ablaze. The fire of the Sepoy Mutiny was not confined to the cities; like a wild beast, it spread into the forests and jungles as well.

Rajarama, head of the household, grew anxious. Looting and plunder everywhere—at some places, the English sepoys were looting, at others, the rebel sepoys. Rajarama received word that a band of sepoys was approaching. He prepared to safeguard his property.

But how was he to protect it? The century-old fortress could not withstand an assault by well-trained, firearm-wielding enemies. The crumbling gateway of the fort would be blown away by a single cannon shot. There was, it is true, a large cannon in the fort, but after years of disuse it had rusted and become useless; the iron hatch at its base was so jammed it could not be opened. As for the few muskets they possessed, they sufficed for hunting deer in the jungle or chasing off thieves, but were utterly inadequate to hold off a band of plundering sepoys.

After consulting with his worthy son, Rajarama arranged to relocate the women and children of the family. A few krosh from the fort, deep in the jungle, lay a Santhal village; his wife, daughters-in-law, and two or three grandchildren were sent there. All the servants and staff went with them; only Rajarama and his son Jayarama remained in the fort. At parting, Rajarama tied a few mohurs into the edge of his wife’s sari. He dared not give more—who knew if, tempted by too much gold, their own people might betray them? After their departure, father and son set about hiding the accumulated gold.

Three days later, a band of sepoys under the command of a firangi officer arrived. It seems Rajarama had intended, after hiding the gold and jewels, to disappear from the fort with his son; but they could not escape. The sepoys appeared suddenly and entered the fort without resistance.
What happened within the fort thereafter, no one knows. Two days later, the sepoys departed. But Rajarama and Jayarama were never seen in this world again. The fort stood empty.

In time, the land grew peaceful once more. Several months later, Rajarama’s family and attendants returned to find nothing left but the stones of the fort; anything that could be taken had been carried off by the sepoys. In several places within the fort, even in the floors of rooms, the sepoys had pried up stones and dug pits—no doubt searching for buried treasure. Whether they found anything is impossible to say, for only Rajarama and Jayarama knew where the treasure had been hidden. Perhaps the sepoys had looted everything; perhaps they found nothing, and so killed father and son before leaving.

For a while, the two helpless women remained in the fort with the children, but the place that had once been a home had now become a crematorium. Gradually, the servants and staff began to fall away, one by one; for a house alone is not enough to sustain life—food and clothing are needed as well. At last, one day, the two widows took the children by the hand and left the fort. Where they went

There is no record of where she found refuge. Perhaps, in Bengal, she found shelter in the home of some distant relative. The abandoned fortress became the dwelling place of jackals.

Thereafter, for nearly sixty years, the history of this lineage lay shrouded in darkness. In the second decade of the twentieth century, two young men of the family once again raised their heads. Rambinod and Ramkishore Singh—two brothers. They grew up in poverty, yet never forgot the pride of their ancestry. The two brothers started a business, and after so long, fortune once more looked kindly upon them. First dealing in ghee, then in iron, they amassed lakhs upon lakhs of rupees.
But the elder brother, Rambinod, did not live long. In the prime of his youth, he died suddenly and mysteriously. Ramkishore continued the business alone and earned even more wealth.

The days passed. Ramkishore married, and children were born to him. Then, at the end of the third decade of the twentieth century, Ramkishore repurchased the ancient ancestral property and built a new house on the second peak beside the fortress. He bought up much of the surrounding zamindari land and settled with his family in the mountain home. The fortress, too, was repaired here and there as a token of its former glory; but it remained as unused and desolate as before.

The old stone-paved road does not end at the foot of the hill; it climbs a little way upward. Where the ascent begins, by the edge of the stone, there is a large well. Nourished by its waters, several great trees have formed a ring around it.

From here, the road climbs for about fifty yards and ends before the gateway. Then, the stone steps, like a serpent’s tongue, fork in two directions: one leads to the arched entrance of the fortress, the other to Ramkishore’s residence.
By the gateway, there is a long shed for keeping the motorcar, and two small quarters for the driver’s lodging. Here reside Ramkishore’s old motorcar and his old driver, Bulakilal.
From here, the steps that ascend towards Ramkishore’s house do not rise straight up, but curve around the flank of the hill. The broad steps reach all the way to the main entrance of the house.

Atop the hill, the land has been leveled into a square, with the large house at its center. The house is surrounded by orchards and flower gardens, and the gardens are enclosed by a fence of thorny creepers. Standing here, one can see, just a hundred cubits away, the smoke-colored fortress on the highest peak; to the north, six miles distant, the town appears faintly to the eye. To the south, from the base of the ascent, the jungle begins; as far as the eye can see, dense ranks of trees. This forest, too, belongs to Ramkishore. From its sal, teak, and ebony, he earns a considerable income.

When Ramkishore first took up residence in this house, he was not yet forty; his body was still strong and healthy. Yet, perhaps because there was no longer any need to toil for wealth, he willingly embraced this seclusion. With him came his wife, two sons, a daughter, a host of servants, and the venerable steward Chandmohan Dutta.
In time, another son and daughter were born to Ramkishore. Then his wife passed away. The burden of raising five children fell upon Ramkishore alone.
Durgarahasya 285

The sons and daughters began to grow up. Yet Ramkishore could not find happiness in his family life. As the children matured, their true natures started to reveal themselves. Perhaps, being cut off from all society in this wild place had warped their characters. The eldest son, Banshidhar, was fiercely hot-tempered; when angered, he lost all sense of reason. After passing his matriculation at the local school, he went to study at Berhampore College. But within a few months, he was forced to leave, having committed some grave and heinous misdeed. The college authorities did not disclose the nature of his crime; one of the professors, an old childhood friend of Ramkishore, managed to hush up the affair. Even Ramkishore himself never learned the truth. Perhaps, if he had, disaster would have followed.

Banshidhar returned home and declared to his father that he would study no more; from now on, he would look after the zamindari. Ramkishore, irritated, scolded him, but did not force his will upon his son. Banshidhar began to supervise the estate. The estate manager, Chandmohan Dutta, took him by the hand and taught him the work.

In due course, Ramkishore arranged Banshidhar’s marriage. But only a few months after the wedding, the bride met with an untimely death. Banshidhar was not at home, having gone to inspect the estate. One morning, the bride was found missing from the house. After much searching, her body was discovered wedged in the crevice between two peaks. It seemed that, for some reason, she had left her room at night and gone to the edge of the ravine, where she slipped and fell. The death was mysterious. On returning, Banshidhar was shattered by the news of his wife’s death; in a frenzy of rage, he did not hesitate to accuse his siblings. From that time on, his violent nature seemed to grow even more fearsome.

Ramkishore’s second son was Muralidhar, a year and a half younger than Banshidhar. He was as thin as a lizard, his bones jutting out, his face sharp as a dhuti needle; his eyes were so terribly crossed that it was impossible to tell where he was looking. On top of that, a crooked spine bent his frail body like a bow. Muralidhar had been crippled since birth. His character was the opposite of Banshidhar’s; he was not hot-tempered, but sly and sinister. Once, in their youth, the two brothers quarreled, and Banshi slapped Murali across the face. Murali had no strength to retaliate. He swallowed the blow; but a few days later, Banshi was suddenly seized by such violent vomiting that his life was in danger. Nothing could be proved against Murali, but ever since then, Banshi never dared lay a hand on him again. He contented himself with threats and bluster.

Muralidhar never learned to read or write, and with that appearance, his father did not arrange a marriage for him. He kept to himself, chewing betel and areca nut day and night. He had a personal servant named Ganpat. Ganpat was Muralidhar’s contemporary; short and stocky, with a round face and equally round eyes, his eyebrows shaped like half-moons. His face always seemed absorbed in a childlike wonder. Yet, few were as wicked as he. There was no misdeed beyond Ganpat’s capacity; from abducting women to burning down houses—if his master commanded, he would do it all. The bond between master and servant was inseparable. It was said that together, they had committed many crimes, but never once were they caught.

Ramkishore’s third child was a daughter, Haripriya. She was about four years younger than Muralidhar; fair to look at, with no physical deformity. But her gaze seemed poisoned. Her mind, too, was steeped in the venom of envy. Haripriya could not bear the sight of her brothers. She was ever seeking out faults, quick to take offense at the slightest slip, and always ready with a biting retort.

This was the nature of Haripriya. After Banshidhar’s marriage, when the new bride entered the household, Haripriya’s fires of jealousy blazed twice as fiercely. The bride was a gentle soul, timid by nature; at every step, Haripriya found fault with her, humiliating her, wounding her with barbed words until she was utterly battered.

Then, suddenly, the bride died. A few months after this calamity had passed, Ramkishore arranged his daughter’s marriage. Realizing she would not be able to manage a prosperous marital home, he carefully chose a poor boy for her. The boy’s name was Monilal; he was well-educated, having passed his B.Sc., healthy, of a calm disposition. After the wedding, Monilal came to reside in his father-in-law’s house.

Whether Haripriya and Monilal’s married life was happy or not could not be discerned from the outside. Monilal was already a reserved young man, and now, as a poor son-in-law living in his wife’s home, even if there was cause for unhappiness, he remained silent. Nor did Haripriya belittle her husband before others. On the contrary, if her brothers made jokes at Monilal’s expense, she would flare up at once.

In one matter, however, the new couple were openly united. After marriage, Monilal became especially devoted to his father-in-law. His relationship with his brothers-in-law was entirely indifferent; he harbored neither affection nor dislike for any of them. But his boundless respect and devotion for his father-in-law was evident in every word and gesture. Haripriya, too, loved her father; perhaps, apart from him, she loved no one else with true feeling. Haripriya did not possess much capacity for love.

After Haripriya came two siblings: Gadadhar, a boy in his teens, and the youngest, Tulsi. Gadadhar was a bit of a simpleton; his intelligence had not matured with his age. His dhoti and scarf were always in disarray, and he would laugh foolishly for no reason. He had no interest in studies; his only pastime was roaming the woods with a slingshot, hunting birds.

In this pursuit, his younger sister Tulsi was his constant companion. But Tulsi’s development was not like Gadadhar’s—if anything, she was a little ahead of her years. Slender of frame, with a delicate, pretty face, and an extremely restless nature. Her daily routine included searching for bird nests or rabbit holes in the jungle at noon, and in all things, she acted as Gadadhar’s guardian. Nothing in the house escaped Tulsi’s watchful eyes; no one could ever say for certain where she was at any given moment. Yet, among all the siblings, Tulsi was perhaps the most straightforward and sensible.

In Ramkishore’s household, apart from his children, there was another dependent whose introduction is necessary. The boy’s name was Ramapati. Seeing his impoverished kinsman, Ramkishore had given him shelter. Ramapati had passed his matriculation; Ramkishore had kept him in the house with the intention that he would tutor Gadadhar and Tulsi. Ramapati was diligent in his efforts, but the meetings between master and pupils rarely took place. Ramapati was a shy, withdrawn boy; the children ignored him, and the rest of the household barely noticed his insignificant existence. Thus, for the sake of two meals a day and a roof over his head, Ramapati lingered in a corner of the house.

The estate manager, Chandmohan Dutta, has already been mentioned. He was five or six years older than Ramkishore, and had been with him since the beginning of Ramkishore’s working life. After Banshidhar took over the management of the zamindari, Chandmohan was, in a sense, relieved of his duties. Yet he kept a vigilant eye on all affairs; all income and expenditure, every account, awaited his approval. The man was exceedingly shrewd and knowledgeable in matters of property; after so many years together, he had become one of the family.
It is true that Ramkishore could not find happiness in his domestic life, but out of affection and...
Durgarahasya 287

With age, a man’s capacity for endurance increases. In his youth, his nature was indomitable and intolerant; now it has softened considerably. Once, he considered manliness the ultimate virtue, but now he does not entirely deny the hand of fate. Though he is not overly devoted to religious rites, he never displays disrespect toward the household gods. His wife came from a staunch Vaishnava family—perhaps her influence was not wholly lost on Ramkishore. At the very least, the names of their sons and daughters still bear the imprint of that heritage.

Yet, on rare occasions, when his patience was truly tested, his formidable inner nature would erupt—like a demon trapped in a pitcher, a fierce and violent rage would blaze forth. In those moments, no one dared stand before him, not even Banshidhar, who would retreat in fear. But his anger never lasted long; it flared up suddenly, only to die down just as quickly.

Eight or nine months after Haripriya’s wedding, at the end of winter, a band of Bedes—nomadic men and women—came and set up camp near the well. With them arrived a motley collection of donkeys, dogs, chickens, snakes, and other creatures. At night, they lit fires, drank liquor, and their women and men danced, sang, and made merry with wild abandon. By day, they cut wood in the jungle, set traps for wildfowl and hares, and used the water from the well as they pleased. The Bede tribe has never been known for its strict morals.

At first, Ramkishore said nothing, but gradually he grew irritated. What worried him most was that Gadadhar and Tulsi, forsaking food and sleep, began to loiter around the Bedes’ tents, their sleepless curiosity undiminished despite repeated scoldings. The elders of the household, of course, openly avoided the Bede settlement; but it could be guessed that, under cover of darkness, some of the servants—and perhaps even some of the masters—ventured there. The Bede women may not have been beautiful, but they possessed a certain bewitching allure.

After about a week of this, one day several Bedes—men and women—came straight to Ramkishore’s main house and laid out their wares: shilajit, musk from the musk deer, snake venom, sulfur-scented soaps, and the like. Banshidhar was present; he drove them away with threats and shouts. Ramkishore ordered that they must leave the area that very day.

The Bedes did obey, but not completely. At dusk, they packed up their camp and moved two or three hundred yards away, setting up again at the edge of the jungle. The next morning, Banshidhar saw this and flew into a rage. Armed with a gun and accompanied by several servants, he stormed into the tents. At his command, the servants began beating the Bedes, while Banshidhar fired his gun into the air. This time, the Bedes truly fled the area.
The trouble was gone, but Nayeb Chandmohan shook his head and said, “Perhaps this wasn’t wise. Those fellows are cunning; they may try to take revenge.”
Banshidhar replied arrogantly, “What harm can they do?”
Chandmohan said, “Who can say? They might poison the well, or set fire to the jungle—”
For some days, everyone remained vigilant, but nothing untoward happened. The Bedes made no attempt at mischief—or if they did, it came to nothing.
Byomkesh Samagra

About a month later, Ramkishore took his family into the jungle for a picnic. This was his annual ritual. A canopy would be set up amidst the trees; the servants would slaughter a goat and begin to cook; the boys, armed with rifles, would roam the forest in search of game and birds. The master would sit beneath the awning and play a few games of chess with Chandramohan. Then, in the afternoon, everyone would return home.

That morning, Ramkishore arrived at the chosen spot with his entourage. A clearing had been made in the dense sal forest; a carpet spread on the earth, the canopy overhead. The cook was lighting the fire, the servants bustling about with preparations. The chauffeur, Bulakilal, sat pounding a heap of hemp leaves in a mortar and pestle—by evening, the bhang would be ready. The sky was golden with sunlight, the breeze gentle and cool in the shade of the sal trees. There was not the faintest sign of ill omen.

The two old men sat beneath the canopy and set up the chessboard; the rest vanished into the forest, each in their own direction. Banshidhar slung his rifle over his shoulder and went one way, while Muralidhar, with his constant companion Ganpat, set off in another, both in search of game. Both were skilled shots. Gadadhar and Tulsi went out together; Master Ramapati followed them at a distance, for it was not impossible for children to lose their way in the dense jungle. Ramkishore had instructed, “Keep an eye on them.”

Son-in-law Monilal, with a book in hand, went to sit behind a tree some distance from the camp. Ramkishore had given him an English book on tantra, which he was reading intently, marking passages as he went. He had no interest in hunting.

That left only Haripriya. She wandered for a while around the cooking preparations, went once towards her husband under the tree, then entered the forest alone. For this one day, everyone was free; after living together in the same house, it was as if they had grown weary of each other’s company, and now, released into the forest, each was savoring a little solitude.

The day wore on. The two elders were absorbed in their game, the occasional crack of gunfire drifted from deep within the jungle, the aroma of cooking filled the air with delight. Through gaps in the leaves, one could glimpse the whitewashed house atop the hill and the ruined fort—not far, at most half a mile away. The shadow of the ruined fort stretched across the ravine and fell upon the white house.

Suddenly, a piercing, continuous scream shattered the lazy murmur of the forest. Both chess players started and looked up. Under the tree, Monilal dropped his book and sprang to his feet. They saw Tulsi, dashing headlong through the dappled light and shadow of the sal grove, screaming at the top of her lungs.
Before Tulsi could reach the canopy, Monilal caught her, gave her a firm shake by the shoulder, and said, “Hey, Tulsi! What happened? Why are you screaming?”
Tulsi stared up at him with wild, glazed eyes for a moment, then, screaming as before, cried out, “Didi! She’s lying under the tree—I think she’s dead! Come quickly—Baba, Uncle, come quickly!”
Tulsi turned and ran back the way she had come; Monilal rushed after her. The two old men followed, stumbling in their haste.
About two hundred yards away, a dense thicket of trees; Tulsi reached the thicket and, under one of the trees—
Durgarohosyo 289
A finger pointed. Haripriya, clad in a saffron-yellow sari, was found lying beneath the dense shadow of the trees, and someone was bending over her body, scrutinizing her closely.
Hearing footsteps, Ramapati straightened up. His face was gaunt with fear, his voice faltering as he said, “Snake! She’s been bitten by a snake!”
Manilal shoved him aside and, with both arms, lifted Haripriya. She was unconscious. On her left ankle, the twin marks of a snake’s fangs—two crimson punctures, side by side.
Haripriya did not survive; she died on the way home.

No one had ever seen a venomous snake in the jungle before. Even now, no snake was glimpsed, but there could be no doubt of its presence; and it was soon accepted as fact that the Bedes were responsible, that they had released snakes or snake eggs into the jungle to exact their revenge. But by then, the Bedes had vanished far away, and no trace of them could be found.

After Haripriya’s death, a heavy, ominous shadow seemed to settle over Ramkishore’s house, like a curse. Of all his children, Ramkishore perhaps loved Haripriya the most; her loss struck him with savage force. Manilal, though a young man of sober temperament, was left utterly distraught by this sudden calamity. The foundation of his newly built life had been shattered by an unforeseen earthquake.

Another who was deeply shaken by this disaster was Tulsi. It was not that she loved her elder sister dearly—indeed, the two sisters were often at odds. Haripriya would scold Tulsi at every opportunity, sometimes locking her in a room. Yet, having witnessed Haripriya’s death with her own eyes, Tulsi seemed to have lost her wits. That day, wandering through the woods, she had spotted a yellow sari beneath a distant tree and gone towards it; then, seeing her sister lying there as she was, she had called out in terror. Haripriya had opened her eyes just once, tried to speak.

Since then, Tulsi had been plagued by confusion. With haunted, anxious eyes, she wandered the house; if anyone questioned her, she would only stare back blankly. There was no doubt that her immature nerves had suffered a grievous blow.

Banshidhar and Muralidhar too had been shaken, though not as deeply. Banshidhar became withdrawn; perhaps, in his heart, he blamed himself for Haripriya’s death—had he not been so harsh with the Bedes, perhaps none of this would have happened. Outwardly, Muralidhar showed no change, but he too had withdrawn into his shell like a turtle. The two brothers found common ground in one thing: both began to look upon Manilal with suspicion, as if he were responsible for Haripriya’s death.

A month after Haripriya’s passing, Manilal went to Ramkishore and asked for leave to depart. With tears in his eyes, he said, “I shall never forget your kindness. But I have no place in this family any longer.”
Byomkesh Samagra

Ramkishore’s eyes, too, grew moist. He said, “Why is there no place for you? The one who has gone is gone; must I lose you as well? That cannot be. You must stay. If the Lord wills, perhaps the bond will be restored.”
Banshidhar and Muralidhar were present. Banshidhar’s face darkened as he stood up; a crooked line of discontent twisted Muralidhar’s lips. The implication was lost on no one.
Manilal remained. More detached and indifferent than before, he continued to live in his former father-in-law’s house.

Thus, two years passed without incident. Ramkishore’s household gradually returned to its former rhythm. Only Tulsi failed to regain her old composure. The shock to her mind had been so grave that her physical and mental growth had come to a standstill. At ten, her body and mind were as immature as a child’s; even at thirteen, she remained unchanged. In short, though she had reached the threshold of adolescence, she lingered in girlhood.

Moreover, another change had come over her. The master she had once neglected without end, she now, for no apparent reason, grew deeply attached to. This brought Master Ramapati more discomfort and unease than joy. For those accustomed to indifference are often bewildered when shown a little affection.

Be that as it may, just as Ramkishore’s household machinery began to move smoothly again, a guest arrived. He was a friend from Ramkishore’s youth. In truth, his bond had been closest with Ramkishore’s elder brother, Rambinod. After Rambinod’s untimely death, his friendship with Ramkishore had waned, but the thread of affection had never quite snapped. He had been a college professor, recently retired. His name was Ishanchandra Majumdar. Some years ago, when Banshidhar was about to be expelled from college for mischief, it was he who had saved him.

Professor Ishanchandra’s appearance was ascetic, gaunt as a hermit, his nature tinged with astringency. Since his retirement, his health had declined, and it seemed he had fallen into financial hardship as well. Remembering their old intimacy, he wrote to Ramkishore: it had been long since he’d seen them, who knew how much time remained, the climate there was said to be good, and so on. Ramkishore replied with a warm invitation, assuring him that the air here was excellent, and that if he stayed a month or two, his health would surely be restored.

In due course, Ishanchandra arrived and took up residence in the house. Banshidhar knew nothing of this; he had gone to oversee the harvesting of the family’s paddy fields. Returning home, he came face to face with Ishanchandra. Banshidhar started as if he had seen a ghost; his face blanched, then slowly flushed red. Approaching Ishanchandra, he said in a low, urgent voice, “You—here?”
For a moment, Ishanchandra gazed steadily at his former pupil, then replied in a dry tone, “I am. Do you object?”
Banshidhar grasped his hand and pulled him aside. “Listen. There’s something I must say.”

What passed between guru and disciple in that secluded corner, no one knew. But it was clear their exchange had not been pleasant, for soon after, Ishanchandra went to Ramkishore and declared his wish to leave that very day. Ramkishore pleaded with him at length; in the end, it was settled that the professor would stay in the durg. A couple of rooms in the durg were still fit for habitation; the professor

There was no objection to the gentleman’s solitary confinement. His meals would be delivered to the fort.

That evening, after installing Ishan Chandra in the fort, Ramkishore returned and sent for Banshidhar. Father and son exchanged words. Suddenly, Ramkishore flared up like a blaze in dry straw, and in a harsh voice, rebuked his son. Banshidhar, however, did not raise his voice; with bloodshot eyes, he listened to the scolding, his anger burning uselessly within.

Thus, Ishan Chandra began his residence in the fort. At night, he remained alone, but during the day, everyone from the house except Banshidhar and Muralidhar would come and go from the fort. Muralidhar was deeply aggrieved with the professor, for by occupying the fort, the professor had seized his secret pleasure-grove.

Another week passed without incident. One evening, as Ramkishore was on his way to visit Ishan Chandra, descending to the gateway and about to take the stairs to the fort, he noticed smoke rising from the cluster of trees near the well. Curious, he approached. Beneath the trees, he saw a sadhu seated before a smoldering dhuni.

The sadhu’s body was smeared with sacred ash, matted locks crowned his head, and his beard and mustache were streaked with grey and black. For a long moment, Ramkishore and the sadhu gazed at each other in silence, eyes fixed and unblinking. Then, from the sadhu’s throat, there burst forth a deep, rolling laugh.

Ramkishore never made it to the fort. He returned and lay down upon his bed. Soon after, a chill seized him, and fever set in. In his delirium, he began to babble loudly. The doctor was summoned. The babbling ceased, and the fever broke. Gradually, Ramkishore recovered. But it became evident that his heart had suffered a grave injury. Previously, his heart had been quite strong.

Another week passed. Ishan Chandra remained in the fort as before. No one attempted to drive the sadhu away from beneath the trees. Once burned, the cow fears even the red clouds; after what had happened with the Bedes, no one wished for a repeat of that misfortune.
Byomkesh Samagra
Uttarkhanda

One morning in the month of Kartik, Byomkesh and I had just finished our tea and eggs in our Harrison Road lodgings and settled down with the newspaper. Satyabati was engaged in household chores inside. Putiram had gone to the market.

After Byomkesh’s marriage, I had proposed to find another place to live; after all, it is a friend’s duty to ensure the newlyweds’ life is undisturbed. But neither Byomkesh nor Satyabati would let me go. And so, for the past four years, we have lived together under the same roof. With Byomkesh, I no longer felt the want of a brother; with Satyabati, I found both a sister and a sister-in-law. Moreover, the prospect of a nephew arriving soon had recently become imminent. Life passed in unexpected happiness and peace.

We divided the newspaper between us. I took the front page, Byomkesh the inside pages. Byomkesh had little interest in the headlines printed in bold on the front; his mind wandered more in the bylanes than the main thoroughfares of the news.
Suddenly, looking up from the paper, Byomkesh asked, “Do you know the name Ishan Chandra Majumdar?”
I thought for a moment and replied, “The name sounds familiar. Who is he?”
Byomkesh said, “He was a professor of history. I was his student for a while in Berhampore. The gentleman has passed away.”
I said, “Well, if you were his student, he must have been old enough to die by now.”
“Perhaps so. But it wasn’t a natural death. He died of snakebite.”
“Oh.”
“Last year, where we went to recover our health, he went there this year. That’s where he died.”

That hill-encircled town in the Santhal Parganas! We had spent a few joyful weeks there; memories of those days, which had begun to fade, returned to me. Mr. Mohidhar, Purandar Pandey, Dr. Ghatak, Rajani—

I said, “But where? In such a vast fort, is it so easy to dig up and find it?”
“It’s not easy. But I believe Ishan Babu had found it; otherwise, the coins in his grasp make no sense.”
Turning the thought over in my mind, I finally said, “If that’s so, then there must be many more coins there.”
“Possibly. And more importantly, if Ishan Babu could find it, then so can we.”
Byomkesh rose and began pacing in the darkness. After a while, as he walked, he suddenly uttered an “Oof!” and nearly stumbled, barely managing to steady himself. I leapt up—
Durgo Rahasya 313
I stood up—"What happened!"
"Nothing, just stumbled a little." The torch was in his hand; he switched it on and cast its beam upon the ground.

What had escaped our notice in daylight now became immediately apparent. A square stone had recently been pried up by someone, and then, with clumsy hands, replaced in its original spot. The stone did not sit evenly; one edge jutted up slightly. In the darkness, Byomkesh had caught his foot on that raised edge and stumbled.
Excited by the sight of the loose stone, I exclaimed, "Byomkesh! Is there a secret chamber to the toshakhana beneath this stone?"
Byomkesh shook his head. "No, the stone is, at most, fourteen inches square. Even if there is a hole beneath, a person couldn't possibly fit through it."
"Still—"
"No, it’s not what you’re thinking. There can’t be a secret entrance to the toshakhana in the middle of an open courtyard. In any case, tomorrow morning we’ll have the stone lifted and take a look."

Byomkesh swept the torch around, casting light in all directions, but nowhere else did it seem that the paving stones had been disturbed. Not far off, the cannon lay where it always had, dust and grime thick beneath it, anchoring it to the floor; there, too, no loose earth or stone was visible.
At that moment, Sitaram arrived to announce that dinner was ready. I glanced at my wristwatch—it was a quarter to ten. I had no idea how silently the hours had slipped by.

We went inside and sat down to eat. I had never known that khichuri and meat, cooked in such a rustic manner, could taste so divine. On top of that, Sitaram had fried omelets. It was a veritable feast.
After we finished, Sitaram took his meal on the veranda. Coming to the door, he said, "Huzoor, if you permit, I’d like to take a stroll around."
Byomkesh replied, "Very well. Where will you sleep?"
Sitaram said, "Don’t worry about that, huzoor. I’ll spread my bedding outside the door and sleep there."
Sitaram departed. We dimmed the light and stretched out on our beds. The door remained open; since there were no windows in the room, closing the door would have made it suffocating.
Lying there, I must have drifted into a light doze, when Byomkesh’s voice roused me. "Listen, I don’t like those pegs."
"Pegs? What pegs?"
"Why are there so many pegs in the wall? Pandeyji gave an explanation, but I’m not convinced."
There was little sense in suspecting pegs at such an hour. I glanced at the clock—it was past eleven. Sitaram had not yet returned from his rounds.
"Go to sleep now; think about the pegs tomorrow," I said, turning over on my side.

I had fallen into a deep sleep. Suddenly, with a sound like a bomb exploding right by my head, I jolted awake and sat up. For a moment, I could not fathom where I was.

As my sense of time and place returned, I saw Byomkesh shining his torch outside the door, where shards of broken pots and pitchers lay scattered like the remains of some shattered vessel. Then, torch in hand, Byomkesh darted out of the room with great urgency. “Ajit, come—” he called.
I, too, rose in a disheveled hurry and followed him; whether he was pursuing someone or fleeing from danger, I could not tell. Wherever the beam of his torch swept, I ran after it.
At the gateway, Byomkesh cast his light upon the stairs. As I caught up to him, I saw a man rushing up the steps. As he drew near, I recognized him—it was Sitaram.
Byomkesh asked, “Sitaram, did you see anyone coming down the stairs?”
Sitaram replied, “Yes, huzoor, I was coming up when I suddenly collided with someone. I tried to catch him, but he slipped out of my grasp and ran off.”
“Did you recognize him?”
“No, huzoor, I couldn’t see his face in the dark. But as we collided, a foul curse escaped his lips, and from the sound of it, I’d say he was a low-caste Hindustani. But what has happened, huzoor?”
“That I do not yet know for certain. Come and see.”

We returned. In front of the room, the shards of broken pots were strewn about. Byomkesh said, “Look there. I was awake and heard very light footsteps outside. I thought perhaps you had returned. Then, suddenly, the crash—”
Sitaram picked up a piece of broken earthenware and sniffed it. He said, “Huzoor, please, quickly get up onto the bed.”
“Why? What is it?”
“A snake. Someone brought a snake here in a pot covered with a lid and smashed it right here. Give me the torch, I’ll search for it. The snake must be nearby.”
Without delay, we climbed onto the bed, for in the dark of night, bravery is no match for a snake. Sitaram took the torch and began searching outside.
Byomkesh, lighting the lantern, said, “Now I understand what kind of fear they tried to instill in Ishanbabu to drive him away.”
“But who was the man?”
“That is hard to say for now. It could be Bulakilal, it could be Ganpat, or even the Sannisi Thakur.”
At that moment, we heard Sitaram’s sudden burst of laughter. He called out, raising his voice, “Huzoor, come and see over here. There’s nothing to fear.”
Cautiously, we climbed down and went to Sitaram. In one corner of the house, a brown snake lay coiled, writhing. The snake was injured, unable to escape, twisting and turning under the harsh light.
Sitaram laughed and said, “A dhamna snake, huzoor, harmless. Seems someone is trying to—”
Durg Rahasya 315
“Dillagi is going on.”
Byomkesh said, “Dillagi indeed. But now, what are we to do with the snake?”
“I’ll take care of it.” Sitaram fetched a brass lid with holes for covering food and pressed it down over the snake. “Let it be for tonight. We’ll see about it tomorrow.”
We returned to our room. Sitaram busied himself spreading his bedding before the door. Midnight had just struck.
Byomkesh said, “Sitaram, where were you till so late at night, and what were you doing? Tell me now.”

Sitaram replied, “Huzoor, I went down to the courtyard. There I saw Bulakilal, high on bhang, sleeping in his own quarters. I had hoped to get some information out of him, so I’d befriended him earlier in the evening. I tried shaking him awake, but Bulakilal wouldn’t stir. What to do? I thought I’d go pay my respects to the Sadhu-baba.
“Sadhu-baba was awake, and seemed pleased to see me. He asked me many questions—who you all were, why you’d come here, things like that. I told him you’d come for a change of air.”
Byomkesh said, “Good, good. What else did you talk about?”

Sitaram replied, “A lot of idle chatter, huzoor. Circling around, I finally brought up the subject of Professor Sahib’s death. At that, Sadhu-baba flew into a rage. I saw he harbored a deep grudge against the landlord and the Nayeb-babu. He kept repeating, ‘They’ll be ruined, they’ll be ruined.’”
“Is that so! A most ungrateful sadhu, I see. And then?”
“Then Sadhu-baba packed a chillum of ganja. He offered me some as prasad.”
“You smoked the ganja?”
“Yes, huzoor. One cannot refuse the Sadhu-baba’s prasad.”
“True enough. And then?”
“Then Sadhu-baba spread out his blanket and lay down to sleep. I left. On my way back, I bumped into that man on the stairs.”
Byomkesh said, “Tell me, Sitaram—when you were coming back, did you see Bulakilal?”
Sitaram replied, “No, huzoor, I didn’t see him. But as I passed by the courtyard, I heard his loud snoring coming from his room.”
Byomkesh said, “Well, then it seems whoever brought the snake’s pot, whoever he may be, it was neither Bulakilal nor Sadhu-baba. I hope he won’t return tonight—now get some sleep.”

In the morning, we found the snake under the lid had died during the night; perhaps it had been gravely injured when the pot broke. Sitaram lifted it on the end of a stick and threw it outside the fort walls. We too went up onto the ramparts and made a circuit. We saw that, though the rampart was not entirely unbroken, there was no secret entrance to the fort except for the main gateway. Below the rampart lay a sheer drop into unfathomable depths.
Around eight o’clock, leaving Sitaram at the fort, Byomkesh and I went to Ramkishore-babu’s house. Ramapati greeted us on the main veranda. “Come in. The master will be here any moment—”

Facing the wall, he sat, arranging rows upon rows of tobacco in small clay bowls. Perhaps he preferred to finish the day’s work in the morning itself. Byomkesh waved his hand, dismissing Ramapati. We entered the room; Byomkesh quietly pulled the door to.
Our sudden arrival startled Chandmohan, who sprang to his feet in alarm, a shadow of fear flickering in his cunning eyes. He stammered, “Who—wh-who are you—?”
Byomkesh seated himself at the corner of the takhtposh and said, “Chandmohan Babu, I have a few questions for you.” His tone was not particularly gentle.
Recovering from his initial shock, Chandmohan wiped his hands on his gamchha and asked, “What is it?”
“It’s about something from long ago. How did Rambinod die?”
Chandmohan’s face grew gaunt. He fell silent for a moment, then muttered in a half-whisper, “I can’t say anything—I’m just the steward of this house—”

Byomkesh’s voice turned grave. “Chandmohan Babu, you know my name; it does not go well for those who try to hide things from me. There is proof you were present at the time of Rambinod’s death. Tell me everything—how did he die?”

Chandmohan shot Byomkesh a sharp, furtive glance, then slowly came to sit at one end of the takhtposh. In a dry voice, he said, “Since you insist, I have no choice but to speak. I will tell you what I know.”
He wiped his face with the damp gamchha and began—

“In the winter of 1911, we were in Munger. Rambinod and Ramkishore were in the ghee business then, sending consignments to Calcutta. They had a large warehouse. I was an employee, stationed at the warehouse. The two brothers would come and go.

“Suddenly, one day, plague broke out in Munger. People were dying and fleeing in panic; those who survived abandoned their homes and ran. The city became deserted. Rambinod and Ramkishore were in Munger at the time, and they were in great trouble. There was merchandise worth sixty or seventy thousand rupees in the warehouse—impossible to abandon it; thieves would surely take everything. The three of us consulted and decided to rent a boat on the Ganga and live there, taking turns to go ashore each day to check on the warehouse. Whatever fate had in store, so be it. There was one advantage—the warehouse was not far from the river.

“Rambinod had a childhood friend who taught at a school in Munger—Eshan Majumdar. Eshan died of snakebite some years ago. He too joined us on the boat. There were no boatmen, only the four of us—the boat was quite large; we cooked and lived on it. Sometimes we would anchor at a sandbar in the middle of the Ganga and spend the night there. Our only contact with the city was the daily trip to check on the warehouse.

“Ten or twelve days passed like this. Then, one day, Rambinod caught the plague. He had gone into town and returned with a fever. We took the boat to the sandbar and brought Rambinod ashore. There was no treatment for plague, and in the middle of the river, where would we find medicine, where a doctor? Rambinod died the very next day.”
Byomkesh asked, “What did you do then?”
Chandmohan replied, “We didn’t have the courage to stay any longer. Abandoning the warehouse, we set the boat adrift and fled to Bhagalpur.”
“Did you perform Rambinod’s last rites?”
Chandmohan wiped his face with a gamchha and said, “There were no means for a cremation; the body was set afloat in the waters of the Ganga.”
“Come, let’s return. Our work here is finished for now.”
As we walked towards the stairs, I asked, “What do you think? Did Chandmohan tell the truth?”
“He lied a little. But it doesn’t matter.”

Just as we were about to descend the stairs, I noticed Tulsi a short distance away, under the shadow of a tree, lost in her own little world of play. So absorbed was she in her solitary game that she did not even notice us. Byomkesh walked over and stood beside her. She looked up at him with wide, startled eyes. Byomkesh smiled gently and said, “Your name is Tulsi, isn’t it? What a sweet little face you have.”
Tulsi continued to stare at him, unblinking. Byomkesh said, “We’re staying in the Durga. Why don’t you come visit us? Come—I’ll tell you many stories.”
Tulsi kept gazing at him, offering no reply. We walked away.

Back at the Durga, we took a moment to recover from the fatigue of climbing up and down the stairs. Lighting a cigarette, Byomkesh said, “Ramkishore-babu has gone to register the deed. If it goes through, there’ll be a commotion in their house; Banshi and Murlidhar might want to rent a place in the city. Before that happens, this business needs to be settled once and for all.”
I asked, “Byomkesh, do you understand anything? The more I see, the more tangled it all seems.”

Byomkesh replied, “A vague picture is beginning to form on the screen of my mind. It’s not a small picture; many people, many incidents, many conflicts are woven into its shape. This drama began a hundred years ago, and it still hasn’t ended. —By the way, I’d forgotten about that loose stone from last night. Come, let’s see if there’s a hole beneath it.”
“Let’s go.”

A thin crust of lime and brick dust had formed atop the stone, unlike the smoothness of the surrounding stones. Byomkesh examined it and said, “It looks as though the stone was lifted and then replaced upside down. Come, let’s try to lift it.”
We tried to lift it with our fingers, but the stone wouldn’t budge. Then Sitaram was called. Sitaram, ever resourceful, brought a crowbar and pried the stone up.
Beneath the stone, there was no hole—just solid lime and brick dust. Byomkesh examined the underside of the stone and said, “Look here, there’s Urdu-Farsi script!”

I saw that several lines of foreign script had been engraved on the stone. The carving was not very deep, and dust had settled into the grooves, making the writing almost illegible. Suddenly Byomkesh said, “I think—wait, let me fetch Ishan-babu’s notebook.”

Byomkesh had kept Ishan-babu’s notebook with him. He brought it and began to compare the page with the Persian writing to the inscription on the stone. I looked as well. Though I could not make out the meaning, it was immediately clear that the style of both writings was the same.
Byomkesh said, “That’s enough. Let’s go.”
We replaced the stone in its original place and returned to the room to sit down. Byomkesh asked, “Do you understand the matter?”
“You explain it clearly,” I replied.
“Recall what happened a hundred years ago. When he heard the sepoys were coming, Rajaram sent his family away. Only he and Jayaram remained in the fort. Then, father and son hid all their treasures.

“But after hiding the gold and jewels, Rajaram grew fearful. If the sepoys killed them, how would their wives and family ever recover the treasure? So he inscribed a coded message on the stone—written in a language not everyone could decipher. Then he smeared it with dust and mud to obscure the writing, so the sepoys wouldn’t easily notice it.

“The sepoys found nothing when they arrived. In their rage, they killed both father and son and left. Later, when Rajaram’s family returned, they too could not discover where he had hidden the treasure. No one noticed the Persian cipher carved into the stone slab.”
I said, “So you believe Rajaram’s treasure is still hidden in the fort?”
“That’s what I think. Unless, of course, the sepoys tortured Rajaram and Jayaram into revealing the hiding place—if so, then there’s nothing left.”
“And then?”

“And then, a hundred years later, Professor Ishan Majumdar arrived. A scholar of history, fluent in Persian; moreover, he had heard the story of the fort from his friend Ram Binode. He began his search—not openly, but in secret. How far his clandestine investigation progressed, I do not know, but he did discover one thing: the cipher carved into the stone. He carefully copied it into his notebook, and then turned the stone over so no one else would see it. After that—after that, what happened is exactly what we must now uncover.”

Byomkesh lay down on the bed, staring up at the ceiling. I too drifted into scattered thoughts. Perhaps Pandeyji would not come at this hour… What news of Satyabati in Calcutta… Why did Byomkesh suddenly speak to Tulsi with such tenderness? The girl is fourteen, but looks no more than ten…

A shadow fell near the door. Turning, I saw Tulsi and Gadadhar. In Tulsi’s eyes was a mixture of fear and curiosity—perhaps she hadn’t dared to come alone, so she had brought Gadadhar with her. Gadadhar, however, showed not the slightest trace of fear or shyness; spinning a top in his hand, his mouth twisted in a mischievous, ear-to-ear grin. Seeing me, he said with a laugh, “He he, Tulsi’s going to marry the son-in-law—he he he—”

With lightning speed, Tulsi turned and slapped him across the face. Gadadhar stood for a moment, cheeks puffed out, then, his face solemn, he left the room, spinning his top as he went. Clearly, he was well accustomed to being slapped by his younger sister.
Byomkesh gently invited Tulsi into the room, but she hesitated, clutching the doorpost. Byomkesh then took her by the hand and seated her on the bed.

Still, Tulsi’s fear did not subside; she sat with the tense posture of a startled fawn. Byomkesh began to speak to her in a soft, friendly tone, as if to an equal. A few words of gentle teasing, stories of girls’ games, doll weddings, and other amusements—gradually, as she listened, Tulsi’s fear began to melt away. At first…

After a few monosyllabic replies—‘hmm’, ‘no’—she began to speak more freely. Within fifteen minutes, an easy camaraderie had blossomed between Tulsi and us. Sitaram replied, “Yes, huzoor. Bulakilal has gone to town with the gentlemen, I’ll ask him when he returns.”

Byomkesh replied, “Poison! Don’t you think we need to find out where the snake venom came from?”
“Oh—”
At that moment, Pandeyji arrived. A binocular hung from his shoulder by a leather strap. Byomkesh said, “What’s this? Why the binoculars?”

Pandeyji replied, “Brought them for you, in case you need them. I couldn’t come in the morning, got caught up with work. So I set out early this afternoon. “Their court business all settled?”

As he listened to the news, Pandeyji grew visibly excited. When the account was finished, he said, “There’s no doubt anymore. Ishan Babu discovered the hidden treasury, and that’s why someone killed him. The question now is, who could have done it?”
Byomkesh said, “Anyone from Ramkishore Babu to Sannyasi Thakur could have done it. But that’s not the only question. There are others.”
“Such as?”

“For instance, where did the poison come from? Snake venom isn’t something you find just anywhere. Then, consider this: to inject snake venom into the body, you’d need a device that leaves marks just like a snake’s fangs.”

“No. Besides, two marks side by side—”
“That’s nothing. If the patient has already lost consciousness, is it so hard to prick twice in the same spot?”
“That’s true. What other questions?”
“And, if Ishan Babu did find the secret treasury, then where is it?”
“Surely, it’s somewhere in this fort.”
“Not just in the fort, it’s within this very house. The way Murlidhar tried to frighten us with snakes—”
The Mystery of the Fort 323
“Why is someone trying to drive us away? What could be the reason?”
Pandeyji looked sharply. “Murali Dhar?”

Byomkesh replied, “He may have some other motive. The main point is, before Ishan Babu arrived, no one knew about the toshakhana. After that, someone else found out—besides Ishan Babu—and murdered him. But I believe they couldn’t move the loot.”
“How can you be sure?”
“Look, no one likes that we’re staying in the fort. What does that mean?”
“I understand. So, first we need to find the toshakhana. Have you thought about where it might be?”
Byomkesh smiled slightly and said, “Since yesterday, a suspicion has been circling in my mind—”
I said, “The pegs!”
At that moment, Sitaram came in to clear away the tea things. Byomkesh glanced at him and said, “Bulakilal has returned!”

Gripping the pen like a dagger, he raised his eyes to Byomkesh. The hatred and fury in that gaze were indescribable. Monilal bared his teeth and hissed, “Here’s the pen. Want it? Come, take it.”

Ramkishore gazed around him, bewildered and desperate. Byomkesh walked to the door.

Work had slowed to a trickle for Byomkesh. This was nothing new for him; but this time, the length and unbroken monotony of inactivity had begun to drive us both to distraction. On top of that, Khoka and Satyabati were away from home. In desperation, we had finally resorted to playing chess.

I knew chess reasonably well; in fact, I had taught Byomkesh how to play. At first, he lost easily; gradually, it became difficult to checkmate him. At last, the day arrived when he defeated me in a major match.

It is said that there is no shame in being bested by one’s son or pupil. Yet, when the person you taught to move the pieces just a few days ago manages to beat you, you cannot help but doubt your own intellect. My heart was no longer at peace.

To make matters worse, the heat had become unbearable. Ever since that morning in mid-Chaitra, when I awoke drenched in sweat, the temperature had only climbed higher over the past month and a half. There had been a shower or two, it’s true, but those only seemed to intensify the oppressive heat, like the black armor of Krishna. Running the fan day and night brought no relief; it felt as if I were sitting, my whole body drenched in syrup from a rasgolla.

In this state of physical and mental despondency, one morning I spread the chessboard on the takhtposh and sat down to play. Byomkesh had almost completed his arrangement for a bishop’s wheel, while I, excessively agitated, was sweating profusely—when suddenly, we were interrupted.
A soft but insistent knock at the door. Not the postman; his knock had a certain reckless urgency. Then who? We looked at each other with eager anticipation.
After all this time, could it be that a new mystery was about to arrive?
Byomkesh quickly slipped on his panjabi and hurried to open the door. Meanwhile, I threw a light shawl over my bare body and composed myself.

Standing outside was a middle-aged gentleman. Of medium build, solidly put together, with a sharp, clean-shaven face and rimless, smoky spectacles. He wore immaculate white pantaloons and a sleeveless silk kurta. No socks on his feet, only braided leather Grecian sandals. His appearance was neat and precise.
In a refined voice, he said, “Byomkesh Babu—?”
